questions.q: Why can't a trigger make an HTTP callout directly?
options: Triggers run inside a pending DML transaction, and callouts aren't allowed from that kind of synchronous context
Triggers don't support any Apex code execution at all
HTTP callouts require a Visualforce page to initiate them
There is no actual restriction — triggers can call out directly with no issue
questions.explain: Salesforce blocks callouts from a context with an open DML transaction, like a trigger, so the platform never leaves a database transaction open while waiting on a slow external HTTP call.

questions.q: What is a mixed DML error?
options: A syntax error caused by mixing SOQL and SOSL in the same method
An error thrown when a single transaction performs DML on a setup object (like User) and a non-setup object (like Account) together
An error thrown whenever a batch size larger than 200 is specified
An error that only occurs when running Apex tests, never in production
questions.explain: Salesforce disallows combining DML on setup objects (such as User or GroupMember) with DML on regular objects (such as Account) inside one transaction, throwing a mixed DML error.

questions.q: A requirement is to update every Contact across an org with two million Contacts missing a required field. Why can't this run in a single synchronous transaction, no matter how the code is written?
options: Synchronous transactions have a small, fixed governor-limit budget that can't scale up to cover that volume of records in one transaction
Apex cannot query more than 10 Contacts total across the org's lifetime
Updating a Contact record is technically impossible in Apex
Synchronous Apex can only run during business hours
questions.explain: A single synchronous transaction's governor limits (SOQL queries, DML rows, heap, CPU time) are fixed and relatively small — they cannot be stretched to cover millions of records, which is exactly the problem Batch Apex's per-chunk transactions solve.

questions.q: Even when a secondary task like sending a confirmation email technically fits inside governor limits, why might a developer still move it off the main synchronous transaction?
options: To keep the user-facing save or page load fast, instead of making the user wait on work that doesn't need to finish before their action completes
Because governor limits don't apply to email-sending code at all
Because synchronous Apex cannot send emails under any circumstance
Because asynchronous jobs are always billed separately from synchronous ones
questions.explain: Even work that fits comfortably inside governor limits can still slow down the user's save or page load. Pushing non-essential work asynchronously lets the user's action finish immediately while the extra work completes a moment later.

questions.q: Which of the four reasons covered in this lesson maps most directly onto needing Scheduled Apex specifically?
options: Needing to avoid a mixed DML error on a setup object
Needing a job to run on a recurring cadence rather than in direct response to a user action
Needing to make a callout from inside a trigger
Needing to stay under the heap size limit for a single record update
questions.explain: Scheduled Apex exists for jobs that need to run on a recurring schedule independent of any specific user action — the other three reasons (callouts from triggers, mixed DML, and large-volume processing) map to future/Queueable methods and Batch Apex instead.
